fetched_contents.text: A Review of Motion-Preserving Cervical Spinal Implants and Fusion Constructs Abstract Spinal fusion remains a common surgical treatment for degenerative cervical spine pathology. By eliminating segmental motion, fusion alters spinal biomechanics and redistributes mechanical loads to adjacent levels. These changes contribute to adjacent segment degeneration (ASD). Motion-preserving spinal implants have been developed to address these limitations. Cervical disc arthroplasty (CDA) is the most widely used example. Such devices aim to maintain physiologic kinematics while preserving segmental stability. Their biomechanical behavior varies with implant design, material properties, and constraint characteristics. Previous research does not holistically compare fusion with motion-preserving treatments on the spine, resulting in an incomplete understanding of when motion-preserving devices should be considered in treatment over fusion constructs and which specific motion-preserving implants are most appropriate. This narrative review synthesizes experimental, computational, and clinical studies comparing rigid fusion constructs to motion-preserving technologies in the cervical spine. Emphasis is placed on segmental range of motion, load transmission, intradiscal pressure, facet joint forces, and adjacent-segment mechanics. By comparing effectiveness across motion-preserving treatments, alongside their effectiveness to fusion constructs, we found that CDA more closely preserves near-physiologic motion compared to fusion. Taken together, this review underscores the importance of biomechanics-informed implant design for guiding future innovation in spinal implant technologies. Keywords: cervical spine biomechanics, motion-preserving spinal implants, spinal fusion, adjacent segment degeneration, range of motion, finite element analysis, load transmission 1. Introduction 1.1. Clinical Role of Spinal Fusion Anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF) remains one of the most commonly performed spinal procedures worldwide, with more than 100,000 cases performed annually in the United States alone [1]. Clinically, fusion is most frequently indicated for cervical radiculopathy or myelopathy when clinical and imaging findings support neural compression, and when symptoms are progressive and non-responsive to conservative care. The population-level burden of these conditions is substantial, as population-based data from Rochester, Minnesota, demonstrate an annual incidence of cervical radiculopathy of 107.3 per 100,000 in men and 63.5 per 100,000 in women, with peak incidence occurring between 50 and 54 years of age [2]. 1.2. Biomechanical Consequences of Motion Elimination From a biomechanical perspective, fusion disrupts normal segmental kinematics and redistributes motion and mechanical demand to adjacent spinal levels. Experimental and computational investigations have demonstrated increases in adjacent level range of motion, intradiscal pressure, and facet joint loading following fusion [3]. These changes alter load-sharing mechanisms within the spinal column and are widely implicated in the initiation and progression of adjacent segment degeneration (ASD). Accordingly, the annual incidence of symptomatic ASD following cervical fusion is estimated to range from 1.6% to 4.2% [4]. Furthermore, fusion constructs that terminate adjacent to, but do not include, the C5–C6 and/or C6–C7 levels are shown to be associated with an increased risk of developing ASD [4]. 1.3. Rationale for Motion-Preserving Technologies In contrast to rigid fusion constructs, motion-preserving technologies are spinal implants or surgical approaches designed to maintain or restore physiologic segmental motion at the treated level while providing sufficient stability [5]. Meta-analyses indicate that motion-preserving procedures are associated with significantly lower odds of radiographic adjacent segment degeneration (odds ratio [OR] 2.57 for fusion versus motion preservation) and reoperation due to adjacent segment pathology (OR 3.18) [6]. By preserving spinal kinematics and promoting more balanced load sharing across discs, facets, and ligaments, motion-preserving strategies aim to mitigate the biomechanical factors associated with fusion-related adjacent segment pathology. 1.4. Knowledge Gaps in Cervical Motion Preservation Despite their shared goal of motion preservation, motion-preserving technologies differ greatly in implant design, constraint characteristics, and material properties, resulting in differences in biomechanical behavior. Prior reviews have largely focused on clinical outcomes or radiographic motion metrics, often aggregating motion-preserving devices as a single category. Prior studies have not compared the design-specific biomechanical consequences of various motion-preserving technologies in the cervical spine to fusion constructs at both index and adjacent spinal levels. As a result, it remains unclear when motion-preserving devices should be considered in treatment over fusion constructs, and which specific motion-preserving implants are most appropriate. Accordingly, this work presents a narrative, design-oriented biomechanical review comparing cervical spine biomechanics and motion-preserving technologies to clarify index-level and adjacent-level mechanical effects, inform implant selection, and guide future innovations in spine implant design. 2. Study Design This study was conducted as a narrative literature review to synthesize existing experimental, computational, and clinical evidence describing the biomechanical effects of motion-preserving technologies compared with fusion constructs. A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis Abstract Study design Systematic review and meta-analysis. Objective To compare the clinical, radiographic, fusion and complication outcomes between three-level anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF) and hybrid constructs combining ACDF and cervical disc arthroplasty (CDA). Methods Systematic search of PubMed, Embase, Scopus, and Web of Science was performed in accordance with PRISMA guidelines. Comparative studies evaluating three-level ACDF and three-level hybrid surgery were included. Primary outcomes included neck disability index(NDI), visual analogue scale(VAS) scores, Japanese Orthopaedic Association (JOA) scores, C2-C7 Cobb angle, C2-7 range of motion (ROM), fusion rates, and complications. Random-effects meta-analyses were performed. Heterogeneity and publication bias were assessed using standard statistical methods. Results Twelve studies comprising 1008 patients (553 hybrid and 455 ACDF) met the inclusion criteria. Both surgical strategies demonstrated significant improvements in NDI (P = 0.62), VAS [neck (P = 0.40), arm(P = 0.70)], and JOA (P = 0.97) scores, with no significant between-group differences across clinical outcomes. Hybrid constructs maintained ROM (P = 0.06), and cervical lordosis (P = 0.93) comparable to ACDF. Fusion rates at intended arthrodesis levels were high and similar in both cohorts. There were no significant differences in total, early or late complication rates, although heterogeneity was moderate to high across several outcomes. Conclusion In three-level cervical degenerative disease, hybrid surgery and ACDF provide equivalent improvements in pain, disability, neurological recovery, alignment, fusion success, and complication profiles. Hybrid constructs demonstrated a trend towards greater preservation cervical range of motion without compromising clinical efficacy or safety. These findings support hybrid surgery as a selective, motion-preserving alternative to three-level ACDF in appropriately chosen patients. Level of evidence II. Cervical disc arthroplasty (CDA) was developed to preserve segmental motion while maintaining adequate decompression and sagittal alignment.7-9 Hybrid cervical surgery, combining ACDF at selected levels with CDA at others, has subsequently emerged as a strategy to balance stability and motion preservation in multilevel disease. Biomechanical studies suggest that hybrid constructs may better preserve global cervical range of motion, reduce compensatory hypermobility and maintain sagittal alignment, as compared with multilevel fusion alone.10-14 While ROM preservation is biomechanically beneficial, its translation into long-term clinical outcomes remains incompletely defined. Clinically, hybrid surgery has gained increasing acceptance for 2- or 3-level pathology. Despite this growing adoption, the comparative effectiveness of 3-level hybrid constructs vs 3-level ACDF remains incompletely defined. Available clinical studies report heterogeneous findings with respect to functional outcomes, pain relief, neurological recovery, cervical mobility, alignment, and complication rates.10,15-26 Several prior systematic reviews have evaluated hybrid surgery; however, most have pooled 2- and 3-level constructs, combined heterogeneous surgical configurations, or emphasised radiographic outcomes without comprehensive clinical correlation.27-33 Importantly, outcomes specific to proper three-level procedures (such as biomechanical demands and complication profiles) have not been systematically synthesised in isolation. As a result, uncertainty persists regarding whether 3-level hybrid constructs provide clinically meaningful advantages over conventional 3-level ACDF, or whether potential benefits in motion preservation are offset by concerns related to complications, fusion success and durability. Clarifying these issues is essential for informed surgical decision-making and patient counselling in complex, multilevel cervical disease. We hypothesised that, in comparison with three-level ACDF, 3-level hybrid cervical constructs would a. achieve comparable improvements in pain, disability and neurological function, b. preserve greater global cervical range of motion without compromising sagittal alignment, c. demonstrate similar complication and fusion rates at intended arthrodesis levels. Significant differences were found in reduction of global ROM based on the number of fusion levels (p<0.001). The upper adjacent segment ROM increased over time (p=0.004); however, lower segment ROM did not. Three-level ACDF did not obtain greater amounts of lordosis than did 1- or 2-level ACDF (p=0.003). Postoperative neck VAS scores and NDI were significantly higher for 3-level ACDF than for 1- or 2-level ACDF (p=0.033 and p=0.001). * Conclusion ASD occurred predominantly in multilevel cervical fusion, more frequently in the upper segment of the prior fusion and as the number of fusion levels increased. Patients who underwent multilevel fusion had greater reduction of global ROM and increased compensatory motion at the upper adjacent segment. ASD, which is often clinically silent initially, leads to the development of symptoms and often requires additional surgery at adjacent levels and longer follow-up [2]. Several biomechanical studies have documented a mechanism by which adjacent unfused levels compensate for the loss of cervical range of motion (ROM) in fused levels [3,4]. As the number of fused levels increases, unfused adjacent levels are under heavy pressure to increase changes in ROM [3,4]. A change of cervical ROM after spinal fusion may create pressure changes within adjacent discs and subsequent development of ASD [5]. These findings, associated with segmental instability and degeneration, have been supported in clinical studies [6]. In addition, increasing number of levels fused at the time of index surgery are reported to be correlated with increased rates of ASD [7]. Conversely, some authors insist that the number of fusion levels is not associated with the development of ASD and the need for reoperation [5]. These studies are not conclusive as to whether increased numbers of fusion levels cause accelerated degeneration at adjacent segments, whether loss of ROM at the fused levels could be compensated for by increases in unfused adjacent levels, and whether the alteration of cervical alignment following cervical surgery correlates with pain. From February 2013 to March 2016, we treated 388 patients with ventral cord compression caused by cervical disc protrusion or bony spur. We excluded 141 patients with histories of prior cervical surgery, trauma, infection, neoplasm, or ossification of posterior longitudinal ligaments. Other exclusion criteria were (1) operative level, including C2–3 or C7–T1; (2) more than 4-level cervical degenerative diseases; (3) follow-up less than 24 months; and (4) preoperative ASD. Hybrid surgery is most commonly associated with reduced adjacent segment disease (ASD) when it combines anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF) with cervical disc arthroplasty (CDA), particularly in multilevel cervical disease. The evidence base is strongest for hybrid constructs that replace some fused levels with motion-preserving arthroplasty, rather than for hybrid strategies that simply add limited instrumentation or preserve motion at only one level. A review on motion-preserving cervical implants and fusion concludes that motion-preserving procedures are associated with significantly lower odds of radiographic adjacent segment degeneration and reoperation due to adjacent segment pathology compared with fusion, with an odds ratio of 2.57 for fusion versus motion preservation [N1-F1]. Another source explicitly frames hybrid cervical spine surgery as a strategy that “produced a ROM of the entire operated and adjacent levels close to that of the healthy spine” [N1-R3], which is consistent with the idea that partial motion preservation can reduce stress transfer and biomechanical overload at adjacent segments.

The biomechanical rationale is that fusion eliminates segmental motion and redistributes mechanical loads to adjacent levels, which can accelerate adjacent segment degeneration. A review states that fusion alters spinal biomechanics and redistributes mechanical loads to adjacent levels, contributing to adjacent segment degeneration (ASD), while motion-preserving technologies aim to maintain physiologic kinematics and promote more balanced load sharing across discs, facets, and ligaments [N1-F1]. Another source explains that adjacent motion segment degeneration is a common radiological finding reported in up to 92% of patients undergoing ACDF, with an annual incidence of reoperation, and that preservation of motion at the affected spinal level is intended to prevent increased stress to the spine [N5-R2][N5-R3]. A cervical surgery review also notes that anterior cervical discectomy and fusion is a motion-sacrificing procedure with increased risk of ASD, while arthroplasty preserves motion and reduces complications [N1-R2]. This implies that the core mechanism by which hybrid surgery may reduce ASD is partial motion preservation, which reduces compensatory hypermobility and preserves more normal load distribution.

The strength of evidence for reduced ASD incidence or progression is mixed. The review on motion-preserving cervical implants and fusion is a high-level narrative synthesis of experimental, computational, and clinical evidence, which indicates that motion-preserving strategies are associated with lower odds of radiographic adjacent segment degeneration and lower odds of reoperation due to adjacent segment pathology, but it also notes that prior studies have not holistically compared fusion with motion-preserving treatments in a way that allows definitive conclusions about specific devices or surgical configurations [N1-F1]. The evidence is therefore more supportive of a general association than a strong, direct proof that hybrid surgery universally reduces ASD incidence. The adjacent segment degeneration study in the N3 set shows that ASD occurred in 41 of 165 ACDF patients, with increasing rates in multilevel fusion, and that the upper adjacent segment ROM increased over time [N3-F3]. This supports the idea that more fused levels increase ASD risk, but it also shows that the relationship is not absolute and may depend on the number of levels fused and the adjacent kinematic response. The N6 evidence adds nuance: one meta-analysis found that hybrid surgery compared with two-level ACDF showed better preservation of C2–C7 cervical mobility and reduced adjacent segment ROM, but the same source also states that hybrid surgery did not lower ASD incidence or improve clinical outcomes [N6-R3]. This suggests that reduced adjacent segment ROM is a plausible biomechanical marker of reduced ASD risk, but clinical evidence for lower ASD incidence is weaker or inconsistent.

Overall, the evidence base for hybrid surgery and ASD is strongest for hybrid cervical constructs combining ACDF and CDA, with the clearest rationale being motion preservation and balanced load sharing. The evidence for reduced ASD incidence is moderate to weak, because the available studies often show trends toward less adjacent segment degeneration and less adjacent segment ROM, rather than uniformly lower ASD incidence, and because study design differences complicate direct comparisons [N1-F1][N3-F3][N6-R3].

The evidence on segmental range of motion (ROM) after hybrid cervical surgery is generally favorable but not uniformly conclusive. The most direct evidence comes from a systematic review and meta-analysis comparing three-level hybrid cervical constructs with three-level ACDF. This study reports that hybrid constructs maintained ROM comparable to ACDF and that there was a trend toward greater preservation of cervical range of motion without compromising clinical efficacy or safety [N2-F2]. The same source also notes that fusion rates at intended arthrodesis levels were high and similar in both cohorts, and that there were no significant differences in total, early, or late complication rates [N2-F2]. This suggests that hybrid surgery can preserve global cervical ROM while still achieving solid fusion and safety outcomes.

Other evidence indicates that hybrid constructs may better preserve global cervical ROM and reduce compensatory hypermobility compared with multilevel fusion alone. A search result states that biomechanical studies suggest hybrid constructs may better preserve global cervical range of motion, reduce compensatory hypermobility, and maintain sagittal alignment, as compared with multilevel fusion alone [N4-R1]. Another search excerpt reports that ACDF demonstrated greater loss of cervical spine motion and increased superior adjacent segment motion in a pooled analysis, while a separate study found that hybrid surgery reduced superior adjacent segment motion [N4-R2][N4-R3]. This is important because it suggests that hybrid surgery does not simply preserve motion at the operated level; it also may reduce excessive motion at adjacent segments, which is biologically relevant to adjacent segment disease risk.

The comparison with preserved or non-fused segments is best understood as partial preservation rather than full preservation. A review of motion-preserving cervical implants explains that motion-preserving technologies are designed to maintain or restore physiologic segmental motion at the treated level while providing sufficient stability [N1-F1]. A search result also states that hybrid cervical spine surgery is beneficial to motion preservation of the operated levels and produced a ROM of the entire operated and adjacent levels close to that of the healthy spine [N1-R3]. This implies that hybrid surgery preserves motion at the operated segment, but does not necessarily restore normal motion at all adjacent segments. The evidence also indicates that motion preservation is often combined with some level of segmental stability, which is why the biomechanical rationale is not simply “more motion,” but more balanced motion and load sharing [N1-F1][N4-R1].

Study limitations affect interpretation of ROM outcomes. The review on motion-preserving cervical implants notes that prior reviews have largely focused on clinical outcomes or radiographic motion metrics, and that prior studies have not compared the design-specific biomechanical consequences of various motion-preserving technologies in the cervical spine to fusion constructs at both index and adjacent spinal levels [N1-F1]. This means that many of the reported trends are suggestive rather than definitive. The systematic review and meta-analysis also reports moderate to high heterogeneity across several outcomes, indicating that the results should be interpreted cautiously [N2-F2]. Additionally, the evidence base includes both experimental, computational, and clinical studies, and the cited studies in N2 and N4 do not appear to provide a single homogeneous study design [N2-F2][N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R3]. As a result, reported ROM trends are generally supportive of motion preservation, but they should not be overinterpreted as proof that all hybrid surgeries produce the same degree of preservation.

The N3 study is a retrospective cohort study with 165 ACDF patients divided by number of fusion levels, and it reports radiological measurements and clinical outcomes at follow-up [N3-F3]. This means that much of the evidence on ACDF comes from observational or mixed-method studies rather than randomized controlled trials, and therefore should be interpreted cautiously. The evidence is therefore strong enough to support the association between ACDF and increased ASD risk, but the strength of evidence for causation and for exact incidence rates is limited by study heterogeneity and design flaws.

This implies that hybrid surgery is a middle ground: it is more motion-preserving than full multilevel fusion, but less motion-preserving than pure arthroplasty, and it is designed to balance stability with motion retention.

The difference in adjacent segment disease risk is also generally supportive of hybrid surgery, but not uniformly definitive. The review on motion-preserving cervical implants and fusion states that motion-preserving procedures are associated with significantly lower odds of radiographic adjacent segment degeneration and reoperation due to adjacent segment pathology compared with fusion [N1-F1]. A search result also reports that hybrid cervical spine surgery produced a ROM of the entire operated and adjacent levels close to that of the healthy spine [N1-R3]. The N6 evidence includes a meta-analysis comparing hybrid surgery and two-level ACDF, but it also reports heterogeneous findings and suggests that some outcomes were not meaningfully improved by hybrid surgery [N6-R1][N6-R3]. In addition, the biomechanical evidence base is mixed in design: some studies are experimental or computational, some are clinical, and some are review-based, which makes direct comparisons difficult [N1-F1][N2-F2]. Overall, the evidence supports hybrid surgery as a more motion-preserving alternative to ACDF, with a plausible biomechanical rationale for reduced adjacent segment disease risk, but the evidence is not yet strong enough to establish definitive superiority in all outcomes.

### 1) How hybrid surgery helps reduce adjacent segment disease

Hybrid surgery is most commonly associated with reduced adjacent segment disease (ASD) when it combines anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF) with cervical disc arthroplasty (CDA), particularly in multilevel cervical disease [N1-F1][N1-R3]. The core rationale is biomechanical: ACDF eliminates segmental motion and redistributes mechanical loads to adjacent levels, which can accelerate adjacent segment degeneration, whereas motion-preserving technologies aim to maintain physiologic kinematics and promote more balanced load sharing across discs, facets, and ligaments [N1-F1]. Another source explains that adjacent motion segment degeneration is a common radiological finding reported in up to 92% of patients undergoing ACDF, and that preservation of motion at the affected spinal level is intended to prevent increased stress to the spine [N5-R2][N5-R3]. This implies that hybrid surgery may reduce ASD risk by preserving motion at the operated segment while still achieving decompression and stability.

A key mechanism is partial motion preservation. A review explicitly frames hybrid cervical spine surgery as a strategy that “produced a ROM of the entire operated and adjacent levels close to that of the healthy spine” [N1-R3]. This is consistent with the idea that hybrid surgery does not fully restore normal motion, but rather preserves enough motion to reduce stress transfer and compensatory hypermobility at adjacent segments [N1-F1][N4-R1]. Another source notes that biomechanical studies suggest hybrid constructs may better preserve global cervical range of motion, reduce compensatory hypermobility, and maintain sagittal alignment compared with multilevel fusion alone [N4-R1]. The result is a biomechanical environment that is less hostile to adjacent segments than full fusion.

### 2) Evidence on reduced adjacent segment disease

The evidence for reduced ASD incidence or progression is more suggestive than definitive. The review on motion-preserving cervical implants and fusion states that motion-preserving procedures are associated with significantly lower odds of radiographic adjacent segment degeneration and reoperation due to adjacent segment pathology compared with fusion, with an odds ratio of 2.57 for fusion versus motion preservation [N1-F1]. This is strong support for the general association between motion preservation and reduced ASD risk, but it does not prove that every hybrid strategy reduces ASD incidence.

The evidence is also mixed in more direct comparisons. One meta-analysis found that hybrid surgery compared with two-level ACDF showed better preservation of C2–C7 cervical mobility and reduced adjacent segment ROM, but hybrid surgery did not lower ASD incidence or improve clinical outcomes [N6-R3]. This is important because it shows that reduced adjacent segment ROM is a plausible biomechanical marker of reduced ASD risk, but clinical evidence for lower ASD incidence remains inconsistent. Another source reports that adjacent segment degeneration occurred in 41 of 165 ACDF patients, with increasing rates in multilevel fusion, and that patients with multilevel fusion had greater reduction of global ROM and increased compensatory motion at the upper adjacent segment [N3-F3]. Taken together, the evidence supports the idea that hybrid surgery may reduce ASD risk, but the strength of the evidence for universal incidence reduction is limited.

### 3) What the evidence says about segmental range of motion after hybrid surgery

The evidence on segmental range of motion (ROM) after hybrid cervical surgery is generally favorable but not uniformly conclusive. The most direct evidence comes from a systematic review and meta-analysis comparing three-level hybrid cervical constructs with three-level ACDF. A search result states that biomechanical studies suggest hybrid constructs may better preserve global cervical range of motion, reduce compensatory hypermobility, and maintain sagittal alignment, as compared with multilevel fusion alone [N4-R1]. Another search excerpt reports that ACDF demonstrated greater loss of cervical spine motion and increased superior adjacent segment motion in a pooled analysis, while a separate study found that hybrid surgery reduced superior adjacent segment motion [N4-R2][N4-R3]. This suggests that hybrid surgery does not simply preserve motion at the operated level; it may also reduce excessive motion at adjacent segments, which is biologically relevant to ASD risk.

The comparison with preserved or non-fused segments is best understood as partial preservation rather than full restoration. Motion-preserving technologies are designed to maintain or restore physiologic segmental motion at the treated level while providing sufficient stability [N1-F1]. A search result also states that hybrid cervical spine surgery is beneficial to motion preservation of the operated levels and produced a ROM of the entire operated and adjacent levels close to that of the healthy spine [N1-R3]. This implies that hybrid surgery preserves motion at the operated segment, but does not necessarily restore normal motion at all adjacent segments.

The evidence also indicates that motion preservation is often combined with some level of segmental stability. The review on motion-preserving cervical implants emphasizes that biomechanical behavior varies with implant design, material properties, and constraint characteristics, and that prior studies have not compared design-specific biomechanical consequences of various motion-preserving technologies in the cervical spine to fusion constructs at both index and adjacent spinal levels [N1-F1].
